study.title: Electroacupuncture at Zusanli and at Neiguan characterized point specificity in the brain by metabolomic analysis
study.study_design: Randomized controlled animal experiment (Sprague-Dawley rats) with three parallel groups
study.randomization: Eighteen Sprague-Dawley rats were randomly divided into three groups
study.inclusion_criteria: Male SD rats, weighing 200-300 g, purchased from BioLASCO Taiwan Co., Ltd.

conditions.condition_label_exact: sham acupuncture at Zusanli (ST36) without electric stimulation
conditions.timepoint_exact: 20 min each day for 5 consecutive days; sacrificed immediately after final EA
conditions.tissue_level_reasoning: The condition explicitly states 'subcutaneously inserted' at 'subcutaneous' depth. Subcutaneous insertion means the needle passes through the epidermis/dermis but stops in the subcutaneous fat layer, not reaching muscle or fascia. This corresponds to a superficial insertion (Level 2), engaging cutaneous fibers but not deep mechanoreceptors. The absence of electrical stimulation is irrelevant to depth classification.

extraction_notes.note: This is an animal (rat) metabolomics study, not a human neuroimaging study. No fMRI, PET, EEG, or MEG was performed. The 'neuroimaging' sections have been populated with LC-ESI-MS metabolomics data as the closest analog to what was measured. Brain regions (cerebral cortex, hippocampus, hypothalamus) were studied as dissected tissue, not via imaging.

Sensory/interoceptive responses (deqi) were not assessed or reported. This is an animal study; rats cannot report subjective sensations. Visible muscle twitching was used as a proxy indicator of stimulation adequacy.
Expectancy, blinding, and credibility measures were not assessed or reported. Animal study; not applicable.
Adverse events were not reported in the paper.

In Table 2 (hippocampus), adenosine: PC6 vs Sham p=0.03762, which is <0.05 but the text states 'adenosine levels of the hippocampi were similar among the groups (all p>0.01).' The paper appears to have used p<0.01 as the threshold for significance for this specific comparison.

In Table 3 (hypothalamus), glutamate ST36 vs Sham p=0.0201 (<0.05) and glycine ST36 vs Sham p=0.01504 (<0.05), but the text states 'adenosine, arginine, glutamate, GABA, and glycine levels of the hypothalamus were similar among the three groups (all p>0.05).' This is a discrepancy between the reported text and table values.

For GABA in the cerebral cortex, the text states 'GABA levels of the cerebral cortices were greater in the sham and ST36 groups than in the PC6 groups (both p<0.05).' However, Table 1 shows PC6 vs ST36 p=0.07508, which does not reach p<0.05. The text may be referring to a marginal result or there may be a discrepancy.

For glycine in the cerebral cortex, the text states 'glycine levels of the cerebral cortices were greater in the sham (p<0.05) and ST36 groups than in the PC6 groups.' However, Table 1 shows PC6 vs ST36 p=0.05417, which is borderline and does not clearly meet p<0.05.
The abstract states 'EA at ST6 resulted in upregulation of adrenaline and arginine in hippocampus' — 'ST6' appears to be a typographical error for 'ST36' in the abstract.

The sham group received subcutaneous needle insertion (not intramuscular) at ST36 and ST37, while the active EA groups received intramuscular insertion. This is a procedural difference between sham and active groups beyond the absence of electrical stimulation.

PLS-DA plots (Figure 1B) show group separation for all three brain regions; the separation is qualitatively described but no specific quantitative PLS-DA statistics (R2, Q2, permutation test results) are reported in the text or tables.

Fold-change data are shown in Figure 2 (relative to sham = 1.0), but numeric fold-change values are not provided in tables; only peak area signal counts are tabulated. Fold-change estimates could only be derived computationally from Table data, which was not done per extraction rules.
n=6 per group. Individual animal data are not reported; only group means and RSD% are available from the tables.

The study used dansyl chloride derivatization of brain extracts followed by UPLC-ESI-QTOF-MS (Waters VION) in ESI+ mode. The metabolites identified are adenosine, adrenaline, arginine, GABA, glutamate, and glycine — identified neurotransmitters extracted from specific brain regions.

The paper characterizes findings as 'brain' metabolomics (cerebral cortex, hippocampus, hypothalamus) but the methodology is LC-MS on tissue homogenates, not neuroimaging. The neural_results section has been populated accordingly with metabolomics data categorized by brain region.
